newsitem.title: IRAQ: Baghdad-backed Kurds hit rival targets.
newsitem.headline: Baghdad-backed Kurds hit rival targets.

text.p: Rival Kurdish militias clashed along the Iranian border and again along a strategic road to the stronghold of Sulaimaniya, reports from the field said on Friday.

Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) official Shorsh Jalalal said the rival Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) group struck at PUK positions in five villages around Halabja, 10 km (six miles) from the Iranian border. In 1988 Iraq attacked Halabja with chemical weapons, killing about 5,000 Kurdish villagers.
"But with the support of new forces moved into position, control of three of the villages was regained late last night," Jalalal told Reuters.
The latest attacks marked an expansion of the front in the inter-Kurdish fighting, which took on fresh urgency last weekend with Baghdad's intervention on behalf of the KDP.
The PUK said joint KDP and Iraqi forces began to advance from Arbil along the north route towards the PUK stronghold Sulaimaniya, via Degala and the key town of Koi Sanjaq.

"There has been fighting since this morning there," said Adnan Mufti, a member of the PUK's central committee. "There was shelling of Degala a few hours ago from the Iraqi army and the KDP," he said. He had no further details.

Mufti said the Iraqi army controlled positions more than 20 km (14 miles) from Arbil, including parts of one main road to Sulaimaniya. Control of Degala would offer command of the other main route to Sulaimaniya and cut it off from Arbil.
If they took Koi Sanjaq -- some 10 km (six miles) south of Degala -- and controlled the nearby lake Dukan, they could effectively seal off Sulaimaniya, Mufti said.
"Koi Sanjaq is important to cut off routes from Sulaimaniya," Mufti said. "And 70 percent of electricity in the area, including Sulaimaniya, comes from Dukan."

The PUK leader Jalal Talabani has said he would seek Iranian help if necessary to counter joint attacks by the KDP and Baghdad's forces, which teamed up last weekend to oust the PUK from the main Kurdish city of Arbil.
The KDP said it had killed more than 100 PUK guerrillas in fighting around Arbil, but the PUK said the casualty figures were exaggerated.
"If the Iraqi army continues fighting us, and the Americans do not help us, then we are free to ask anyone," said Mufti.
"If the Iraqi army believes the American action has stopped, they will do anything. We can't stop it alone," he said.

Turkey has indicated that it might also join in the fray, moving forces in to stop anti-Ankara separatists of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) from using the region as a springboard for attacks in southeast Turkey.
Baghdad's move into the Western-protected north drew U.S. cruise missile attacks on targets south of the Iraqi capital. Washington said on Thursday that Iraqi troops had withdrawn.
However, opposition groups report continued Iraqi involvement in support of a KDP advance along the main road toward Sulaimaniya.
A Reuters reporter who toured the region south of Arbil on Thursday saw Iraqi tanks dug in but no evidence that they were engaged in the latest fighting.

Riza Ghafur, head of the PUK foreign relations office, said the KDP and Iraqi troops also continued to shell Chamchamal, on another route to Sulaimaniya. Sulaimaniya is around 120 km (70 miles) southeast of Arbil.
According to the PUK, the joint forces are supported by 100 tanks and rockets and had on Friday morning captured Qushtapa, a town 22 km (15 miles) south of Arbil.
"The tanks are a big problems," Mufti said. "We only have RPGs (rocket-propelled grenades), and that's not enough."
